teaser.text: National Grid plc is an energy-infrastructure company: it owns networks that carry electricity and gas, and it earns mainly by charging for dependable access to them. Its cash flow is easier to understand if you separate the regulated networks from the projects around them, then follow who pays, what gets passed through and what gets invested.

blocks.heading: Where could National Grid's shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted price is 1118.86 GBp in October 2027, 1212.82 GBp in October 2028 and 1318.29 GBp in October 2029. Including dividends, those outcomes represent returns of 0%, 13% and 26% from today’s 1164.50 GBp. By October 2029, the range is wide: 782.89 GBp in the bear case to 1864.75 GBp in the bull case.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for National Grid, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The starting point is FY2026 adjusted net income of £2,892m, excluding the £489m disposal gain. The record is uneven: adjusted net income fell from £3,100m in FY2024 to £2,615m in FY2025 before recovering. The base case applies 8.5% annual growth. It reaches £3,268m in October 2027 and £3,846m in October 2029. The middle figure is £3,545m. This is consistent with the stated 8–10% EPS ambition, while the £13bn FY2027 investment plan and 10% asset-growth target support the regulated growth thesis. The bear case applies 3% growth, reaching £3,023m and then £3,208m, because negative free cash flow and higher finance costs could delay returns. Its middle figure is £3,113m. The bull case applies 12% growth, reaching £3,427m and £4,363m. Its middle figure is £3,867m, requiring approvals, delivery and asset recognition to outperform together.

blocks.heading: How much cash does National Grid really make?

paragraphs.text: Cash capital spending left free cash flow deeply negative. Treating share-based pay as an economic cost makes “real free cash flow” weaker still, because the award dilutes shareholders even though it is not another cash payment. This deficit does not prove that network investment is uneconomic: NGET’s asset-health programme alone totalled about £1.7 billion across RIIO-T2, the UK transmission price-control period. It does show that dividends and expansion require financing beyond internally generated cash.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for National Grid today?

paragraphs.text: Market value is the shareholders’ claim; enterprise value adds lenders’ claim and subtracts cash. Think of a house bought with a mortgage: the house is the whole asset, but the owner’s equity is what remains after the lender’s claim. At 1164.50p on 12 October 2026, National Grid’s market value was £58,538 million. Enterprise value was £101,572 million. Net debt was £44,160 million at 31 March 2026, measured on a different date and under the company’s own definition.

blocks.heading: Does National Grid cover its dividend with cash?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is the cash left after operating needs and capital spending under the company’s definition. It was negative in every year across the five years ending March 2026. The annual deficit reached £4,823 million in FY2026, and dividends paid added £1,623 million to the funding gap. There were no share buybacks.

blocks.heading: What could change National Grid’s dividend?

paragraphs.text: Dividends grow modestly because policy targets CPIH-linked increases, while funding pressure limits the forecast. The base case starts from the latest £0.4849 DPS and grows at 2.5%. It reaches £0.4970 in 2027 and £0.5223 in 2029. The middle figure is £0.5095. The bear case freezes DPS at £0.4849 through 2028 and reaches £0.4946 in 2029. The bull case reaches £0.5019 in 2027 and £0.5377 in 2029, with £0.5195 in between. Negative free cash flow and a planned £6bn increase in net debt explain the restrained assumptions.

blocks.heading: What has National Grid guided for FY27?

paragraphs.text: For FY27, UK Electricity Transmission is expected to add £850 million of underlying net revenue. Depreciation rises £80 million, while costs rise £50 million. Group net finance costs are also expected to rise £200 million, so more network revenue must first absorb higher equipment and borrowing costs.

The new framework targets 8–10% annual compound EPS growth from FY26’s 78.0p through March 2031. The earlier framework targeted 6–8% from the FY25 baseline, so investors need the bridge from network returns, financing, tax and share count—not just the higher percentage.

blocks.heading: What were National Grid's last eight reported periods?

paragraphs.text: The 5 October update offered a mixed signal: regulated businesses were in line with expectations, but about £130 million of upside included one-off fair-value gains from National Grid Partners transactions. The accounts therefore point to a company with genuine regulated growth, improving earnings and strong assets—but also negative free cash flow, rising financing demands and a continuing gap between money invested and useful capacity delivered.

blocks.heading: What should investors watch in National Grid's next results?

paragraphs.text: The first checkpoint is 5 November 2026, when National Grid reports its September half-year. The important evidence will be the composition of earnings: recurring network operations, investment revaluations and cash generation. Because underlying EPS normally favours the second half, doubling the interim figure would mislead.

FERC, the US federal transmission regulator, reduced the base return on equity in New England to 9.57% and ordered historical refunds with interest. National Grid plans to challenge that decision. Separately, transmission owners requested a forward-looking return of 11.39%. The refund concerns money already charged; the proposed return concerns what future investment may earn. One does not cancel the other.
